words: إِنَّمَا يَخْشَى ٱللَّهَ مِنْ عِبَادِهِ ٱلْعُلَمَٰٓؤُا۟
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khashya is fear mixed with reverence, usually arising from knowledge of what is feared; scholars know God best and therefore most revere Him.
rows.anchor: الخشية خوف يشوبه تعظيم ولذلك أكثر ما يكون ذلك إذا كان الخاشي يعلم ماذا يخشى

rows.speaker: قسم
rows.claim: Some say khashya means the most intense form of fear.
rows.anchor: وقسم قال الخشية أشدّ الخوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He illustrates fear as anticipating harm: Aal Imran's command to fear enemies occurs amid the expected danger of battle.
rows.anchor: آية آل عمران في سياق توقع مكروه، في سياق القتال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Man can denote any gender and number; Arabic and Qur'anic usage commonly first treats it as masculine singular, then resumes it according to its intended meaning. This explains the feminine address in the verses.
rows.anchor: يأتي أول مرة بـ (من) بصيغة المفرد المذكر ثم يعقبه ما يوضح المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the Qur'an departs from masculine singular agreement after man, it can reflect the context: more people listen than look, so the latter verb is plural.
rows.anchor: أيّهما أكثر الذين ينظرون إلى الشخص أم الذين يستمعون إليه؟ الجواب الذين يستمعون ولهذا عبّر عنهم بالجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The faʿūl pattern names a material consumed in its characteristic use, as fuel is consumed by burning; the author applies this source-material idea to forms such as shukūr and ghafūr.
rows.anchor: صيغة فعول إذن تدل على المادة التي تُستعمل في الشيء الخاص به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faʿūl has the same form for masculine and feminine and does not take regular sound masculine or feminine plurals; examples include shakūr and ṣubur, shukur, ghufur.
rows.anchor: يستوي فيها المؤنّث والمذكر فنقول رجل شكور وامرأة شكور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghafūr means wholly characterized by forgiveness, which explains why the verse is called the Qur'an's most hopeful verse.
rows.anchor: بمعنى كله مغفرة ولذلك قالوا أن أرجى آية في القرآن هي ما جاء في سورة الزُمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faʿūl is more emphatic than faʿʿāl: ṣabūr gives itself wholly to patience, while ṣabbār denotes a craft or habitual profession.
rows.anchor: هي أكثر مبالغة وتعني أنه يفني نفسه في الصبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghafir discusses creation and God's blessings, including the creation of the heavens and earth, rather than focusing here on monotheism; accordingly, it foregrounds creation in its wording.
rows.anchor: لا على التوحيد فقدم الخلق لذلك فوضع كل تعبير في موطنه اللائق حسب السياق

words: خَالِقُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ
rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmānī explains that al-An'am puts “no deity but Him” first to refute the preceding claims about partners and offspring, while Ghafir puts “Creator of everything” first after discussing creation.
rows.anchor: جاء في البرهان للكرماني قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He cites the different placement of “in God's way” and “with their wealth and lives” in al-Anfal and al-Tawba as further examples in the discussion of word order.
rows.anchor: ومن ذلك قوله تعالى (إِنَّ الَّذِينَ آَمَنُوا وَهَاجَرُوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shorter form in the command to the Prophet concerns his special, individual situation; the fuller form in the rule about orphans expresses a general, continuing, repeated case.
rows.anchor: وهذا خطاب للرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم وهي حالة خاصة به فقال (تبدّل)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al Imran addresses one Muslim community and forbids even a little division, using the shorter form; Shura addresses humanity across the prophets and uses the fuller form for the comprehensive scope.
rows.anchor: فالكلام لكل البشر وذكر كل الأنبياء من زمن نوح إلى قيام الساعة فقال (تتفرقوا)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an uses awṣā for material matters such as inheritance and waṣṣā for spiritual matters such as the religion enjoined on the prophets.
rows.anchor: مثال آخر أن القرآن يستعمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He notes that the one cited use of awṣā with prayer pairs it with zakat: Jesus says God enjoined him to prayer and zakat.
rows.anchor: وفي المرة التي استعمل فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In praise, the Qur'an uses the active “We gave them” wording; in blame, it uses the passive “they were given” wording.
rows.anchor: في موضع المدح يأتي بـ (آتيناهم)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He presents Shura as treating unwelcome events as matters God wills and links its passages on affliction, patience, and adversity to the contrast between transient worldly provision and what lasts with God.
rows.anchor: سورة الشورى عموماً هي في مستكرهات الأمور أي فيما يشاؤه الله تعالى لا ما يشاؤه الإنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God grants daughters or sons according to His will, not human preference; their being granted first and indefinitely counters Arab disdain for daughters, reflected in the cited verses.
rows.anchor: وعند العرب الإناث مما يُستكره من الأمور كما في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author gives another rationale for putting daughters first: doing good to them is protection from the Fire.
rows.anchor: التقديم فيه أمر آخر وهو أن الإحسان إليهن ستر من النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says daughters remain more closely attached to their father because they need a male guardian through life, while a son's care ends at puberty; the father or brother cares for her before marriage, then her husband.
rows.anchor: التقديم له دلالة أخرى وهي أن الإناث ألصق بالأبّ من الذكور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author glosses istawā as rising, becoming upright, and preparing oneself.
rows.anchor: استوى تعني اعتل واستقام وتهيّأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gabriel descends toward the Prophet and draws near after preparing at the highest horizon; this praises Gabriel's readiness and honors the Prophet, whose station requires such preparation and whose mission is great.
rows.anchor: ينزل جبريل - عليه السلام - إلى الرسول - صلى الله عليه وسلم -

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Najm, the highest horizon is the destination of the Prophet's ascent; in Takwir, the clear horizon suits the following denial that he is niggardly with the unseen, just as the Messenger is clear and open.
rows.anchor: أما في آية سورة التكوير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because al-Zukhruf describes the Qur'an in the heavenly Umm al-Kitab with God before its descent, jaʿalnāhu fits; where revelation and descent are at issue, such as the revealed story in Yusuf, anzalnāhu is more apt.
rows.anchor: أمّ الكتاب ليست إنزالاً فتحتاج لـ (جعلناه) وليس أنزلناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arab rhetoricians knew the intended meanings and precise placement of expressions, even where later readers lack that knowledge.
rows.anchor: البلغاء يعلمون ويعرفون في مظانّ الكلام ما لا نعرفه نحن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an's challenge is set at surah length because an individual verse can be one word; even the short Kawthar and Ikhlas are inimitable, so Qur'anic speech of that length is miraculous.
rows.anchor: لم يتحداهم بآية لأن الآية قد تكون كلمة (ألم) و (مدهامتان) آية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He reads al-Nur's context as addressing accusations against women, including false charges and spouses accusing their wives; this frames the verse about impure and good women and men.
rows.anchor: وجدنا أن الكلام في السورة عن النساء ورميهن بالإثم والقذف ورمي الأزواج لأزواجهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author explains that the feminine is mentioned before the masculine because the sexual act begins with women and some women make it a profession, unlike men.
rows.anchor: بتقديم الزانية على الزاني لأن الفِعلة تأتي من النساء أولاً ثم إن بعض النساء تحترف هذه المهنة ولا يحترفها رجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Broken plurals may take masculine or feminine agreement; the author says feminine verbs go with the more numerous group and masculine with the smaller, as in the women around the Aziz's wife and the many Arabs.
rows.anchor: بحسب القاعدة النحوية المعروفة أنه جائز باعتبار أن جمع التكسير يجوز تذكيره وتأنيثه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The smaller group of messengers in Al Imran takes masculine agreement, while the reference to all messengers in al-A'raf is larger and takes feminine agreement.
rows.anchor: المذكورون هم جميع الرسل وهم أكثر من الأولى لذا جاء الفعل مؤنثاً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Coordination can join terms requiring different verbs: one settles in the home, not faith; in Yunus one gathers a plan and assembles partners. An omitted verb is understood, as in the Arab phrase “milk for drinking and dates for eating.”
rows.anchor: الإيمان لا يتبؤأ إنما يتبوأ الدار فهنا عطف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The construction man khalaq in al-Mulk allows both intended parses: man as subject, “does the Creator not know?”, or as object, “does He not know those He created?”.
rows.anchor: إذن (من خلق) تحتمل المعنيين الخالق والمخلوق
